clue.text: Relax free end of chain before having an erection

parts.note: loose means free, unconfined

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, the only one used here

parts.note: last letter of chain
up is slang for aroused

explanation.surface: Advice to unwind, unchained, before a sexual encounter.
explanation.definitionFit: To loosen up is an idiom for becoming less tense, so to relax.

clue.text: (see 26dn.)
More pasty with nuts put before Brenda?

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for with
to nut someone is to headbutt or hit them
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, whose cipher is ER

explanation.surface: Someone goes paler still as nuts are served in front of the Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Nuts is a verb here, a headbutt; Brenda is a running Private Eye joke name for Queen Elizabeth II.
explanation.definitionFit: Pasty describes an unhealthily pale complexion, so more pasty is paler in skin.

clue.text: A showy, though rather tame hand job, this, which won't lead to a bang

definitions.text: A showy, though rather tame hand job, this, which won't lead to a bang

parts.words: A showy, though rather tame hand job
parts.note: surface reading: a sexual favour that ends in no climax

parts.words: which won't lead to a bang
parts.note: setter's reading: a firework held in the hand that fizzes and glitters but never explodes

explanation.walkthrough: Hand job and bang both have a smutty slang sense; in the setter's reading they mean a firework held in the hand and an explosion.
explanation.definitionFit: A sparkler is a hand-held firework of showers of sparks, the tame end of a fireworks display, with no explosion.

clue.text: Old boy caught getting stuck into spout thing

parts.note: OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil

indicators.note: something stuck into another thing is lodged inside it

parts.note: a spout is a jet of water
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A former pupil, caught out, finds himself stuck with some spouting gadget.
explanation.definitionFit: An object is any material item, a general word for a thing.

clue.text: Getting cold in hospital, south Paris did for him

indicators.note: in places the first idea within the second

parts.note: A and E, accident and emergency, the British hospital casualty department
to chill is to grow cold
S is the abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: Someone catches a chill in a hospital somewhere south of Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: Paris reads as the French capital; it is the Trojan prince of Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend the Trojan prince Paris killed the hero with an arrow to his vulnerable heel.

clue.text: Maybe DaVinci Code's opening rot ain't so complicated

indicators.note: complicated means tangled up, so the letters are knotted into another order
an opening is the very first part, so just the first letter of the word is used

parts.note: first letter of Code
taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A sneer at Dan Brown's thriller: its opening is rubbish, not so clever after all.
explanation.walkthrough: The Da Vinci Code is Dan Brown's bestselling thriller; the definition is Leonardo himself, who drew the famous cartoon for The Virgin and Child with St Anne.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonardo made cartoons in the old sense, full-size preparatory drawings for paintings, so he was one kind of drawer.

clue.text: Mate with devil getting runs almost at the start

indicators.note: almost at the start puts the item just after the opening letter of the other word, near its front

parts.note: a fiend is a devil
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: Someone pairs up with the devil and goes off running.
explanation.definitionFit: Mate is informal British for a pal, so a synonym of the answer.

clue.text: Marx making comeback as TV host

indicators.note: a comeback runs things the other way, so the Marx brother's name is read from its end to its start

parts.note: Harpo is the silent, harp-playing Marx brother

explanation.surface: A Marx brother returns from the dead to front a television show.
explanation.walkthrough: Karl is the Marx most solvers try first; it is the comedy brothers Groucho, Chico, Harpo and Zeppo that are meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Oprah Winfrey presented the famous American daytime chat show for twenty-five years.

clue.text: "Bush deal finally kicked out by the people" shock

indicators.note: what is kicked out is thrown out of the word that follows, leaving the rest behind

parts.note: the public is the people at large

indicators.note: finally points at the closing letter of the word deal and nothing else

parts.note: last letter of deal, removed from the word before it
a shock is a thick mass of hair

explanation.surface: A newspaper headline: the voters reject a George W Bush deal, a political shock.
explanation.walkthrough: Bush looks like the US president of 2007; it is slang for the hair it defines, and shock is wordplay rather than the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Bush is a slang word for the tuft of hair growing around the genitals.

clue.text: Sense the acute pain behind the Mensa member?

definitions.note: the question mark flags a jokey example: a member of the high-IQ society, uncharitably seen

parts.note: to smart is to feel a sharp, stinging pain
a behind is the backside, British slang arse

explanation.surface: Someone feels a sharp pain in the backside of a clever clogs from Mensa.
explanation.walkthrough: Mensa is the society for people with very high IQs; a smart-arse is British slang for an irritating know-all.
explanation.definitionFit: A smart-arse is a show-off who flaunts their cleverness, which is the cheeky view of an IQ-society member.

clue.text: (& 23dn/17dn.) Invasion of privacy as justified by tabloid editor frequenting boozer with pointless parasites: "a diversion"

definitions.text: Invasion of privacy as justified by tabloid editor

indicators.note: a point is a compass letter such as east, so pointless says such a letter is dropped from the next word

parts.note: someone frequenting a pub is often found in the place
boozer is British slang for a pub
lice are parasitic insects; the final E (east) goes
an interest is a pastime or diversion

explanation.surface: A dig at tabloid editors who excuse snooping as public duty while they sit in the pub with hangers-on.
explanation.walkthrough: Frequenting the boozer is read as 'in the pub'; parasites are LICE with E, a compass point, removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Tabloid editors defend intrusive stories by claiming publication serves the public good, the standard press defence.

clue.text: Genuine old bastard

definitions.meaning: second meaning: an old word for a child born outside marriage

explanation.surface: Calling someone a real, out-and-out old git.
explanation.walkthrough: Old bastard looks like an insult; the old marks an archaic sense, a natural child being an illegitimate one.
explanation.definitionFit: Natural means unaffected and real, and historically a natural son or daughter was born out of wedlock.

clue.text: Male ex-convict in terrible soap leads as heard on radio

definitions.note: read with the soap before it: the soap one hears on the radio

indicators.note: in places the male ex-convict inside the pair of letters
leads are the front-runners, so only the first letters of the two words are taken

parts.note: first letters of terrible and soap
he is the male pronoun
Jeffrey Archer, novelist and Tory peer, was jailed for perjury in 2001

explanation.surface: A former jailbird turns up in a dreadful soap opera's leading roles.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Archer appeared as himself in The Archers; terrible soap doubles as the definition's soap and the wordplay's letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Archers is the long-running BBC Radio 4 soap opera about farming folk, the world's longest-running drama serial.

clue.text: Silly old fart, one replaced by energy engineer

indicators.note: silly means foolish and muddled, so the letters that follow are muddled into a new order
replaced by tells the solver to swap one letter out for another before going further

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
one is A, as in a single thing; it comes out of the fodder
E is the symbol for energy in physics; it goes in where the A was

explanation.surface: A doddery old buffer is pushed aside for a dynamic young engineer.
explanation.walkthrough: Silly old fart reads as an insult phrase, but silly is the anagram signal and old fart the letters, with A swapped for E first.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Telford was the great Scottish civil engineer of canals, roads and bridges, such as the Menai Suspension Bridge.

clue.text: What emerges from Brighton: inner sign of troubled sleep for Brown soon?

definitions.note: the question mark marks the definition by example: Gordon Brown became prime minister a few days after this puzzle

indicators.note: inner says the next item sits inside the structure named before it

parts.note: Brighton's piers stick out from the seafront into the sea
rapid eye movement, the phase of sleep when dreams come

explanation.surface: Brighton nightmares for Gordon Brown as he waits to take power.
explanation.walkthrough: Brighton is the seaside resort on England's south coast; the puzzle appeared in June 2007, days before Brown succeeded Blair.
explanation.definitionFit: Premier is another word for prime minister, the office Gordon Brown was about to take.

clue.text: (see12ac.)
Place in which irate Cameron starts to be restrained by harassed whips

indicators.note: what is restrained is held inside, so the first pieces go within the other
something harassed is harried and thrown into disorder, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

indicators.note: starts points at the opening letter of each of the two words just before it

parts.note: first letters of irate and Cameron

explanation.surface: An angry David Cameron is kept in line by his party's put-upon whips.
explanation.walkthrough: Whips are the MPs who keep a party's members voting in line; here the word is only letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Ipswich is a county town in Suffolk, eastern England, so it is a place.

clue.text: Not at a loss as to where to put one's balls?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: in profit, having made money

definitions.text: as to where to put one's balls?
definitions.meaning: second meaning: where a snooker or pool player aims to sink each ball

explanation.walkthrough: Not at a loss sounds like not stuck for an answer; it means financially ahead. The balls are billiard balls, despite the smutty hint.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in pocket means to have gained money, and a potted ball in snooker ends up in a pocket.

clue.text: Divine, in Japan for a short time, getting Hello! involved in "Hot Rio" spread

definitions.text: Divine, in Japan for a short time
definitions.note: an adjective defined by its holder: the emperor was held divine until 1946

indicators.note: spread means scattered about, so the letters are scattered into a fresh order

parts.note: hi is an informal hello
taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A celebrity gossip piece: a Japanese star briefly hits Hello! magazine with a sexy Rio photo shoot.
explanation.walkthrough: Hello! is the British celebrity magazine; here it is just a greeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Emperor Hirohito was revered as a living god until he renounced divinity after Japan's 1945 defeat, so only for a while.

clue.text: Guardian arsehole hugging another arsehole with love

indicators.note: to hug is to wrap the arms round, so the first word goes around what follows

parts.note: a cur is a contemptible man
a rat is a despicable, treacherous person
love is zero in tennis scoring, shaped like O

explanation.surface: An insult aimed at a Guardian journalist and a fellow lout, with love.
explanation.walkthrough: Guardian looks like the newspaper; it is a common noun for a keeper.
explanation.definitionFit: A curator is the keeper in charge of a museum or gallery collection, so a guardian of it.

clue.text: The place for office brats?

parts.note: surface reading: spoilt young staff who behave like children at work
setter's reading: the room where working parents leave real small children during the day

explanation.walkthrough: Office brats suggests badly behaved junior colleagues; the brats are literal children of office workers.
explanation.definitionFit: A creche is a nursery for infants, often provided at a workplace so staff can bring their children.

clue.text: Sack Hattersley — this is such an old-fashioned read!

definitions.text: this is such an old-fashioned read

parts.note: to sack a town is to plunder or rob it
Roy Hattersley, the Labour politician and writer, a frequent Private Eye target

explanation.surface: A reviewer demands that Roy Hattersley be fired for writing something so dated.
explanation.walkthrough: Sack reads as dismiss from a job; here it is plunder. The read is Sir Walter Scott's 1817 novel about the Highland outlaw.
explanation.definitionFit: Rob Roy is a Walter Scott novel nearly two centuries old, so a fusty classic of a book.

clue.text: Madonna, say, shoots gangster-style, thanks to Ritchie's introduction

parts.note: in gangster slang to pop someone is to shoot them
ta is British informal for thanks

indicators.note: an introduction comes first, so only the opening letter of the name is used

parts.note: first letter of Ritchie

explanation.surface: Madonna takes up gangster gunplay thanks to her then husband Guy Ritchie, director of gangster films.
explanation.definitionFit: Madonna is an example of a hugely famous singer of pop music, hence the say.

clue.text: (see 12ac.)
Go in for bondage (no time for anaesthetic)

indicators.note: no says the item after it is absent from the word built so far

parts.note: to tether is to tie up, the business of bondage
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone into bondage foregoing the anaesthetic for lack of time.
explanation.definitionFit: Ether was one of the first general anaesthetics, used in surgery from the 1840s.

clue.text: Supporter — but not of cabinet arses?

definitions.text: Supporter — but not of cabinet arses?

parts.note: surface reading: a loyal party backer who is not one of the cabinet's arses, or fools
setter's reading: a seat in the Commons that holds up the bottoms of MPs who are not ministers

explanation.walkthrough: Supporter suggests a political follower; it is a literal seat holding up backsides. Cabinet ministers sit on the front bench, so this one is for the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: In the House of Commons the rear benches seat MPs without ministerial office, so it is furniture supporting non-cabinet members.

clue.text: (& 2dn.) Filth not to be seen here where public loos are quite absent?

definitions.text: Filth not to be seen here
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a district the police dare not enter, filth being slang for police

definitions.text: where public loos are quite absent?
definitions.meaning: second meaning, a pun: a zone with nowhere to go, in the toilet sense

explanation.walkthrough: Filth looks like dirt; it is British slang for the police. The second half puns on go meaning use the toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-go area is a district where police or outsiders avoid entering, typically because of lawlessness.

clue.text: Whore, not skirted, with ring — potential fortune to be got from this

definitions.text: fortune to be got from this

indicators.note: with its skirt, the outer edging, taken off, a word keeps only its inner letters

parts.note: the inside of whore, with its first and last letters stripped
a ring is round, shaped like the letter O
scope is room for development, potential

explanation.surface: A prostitute without her skirt, offering a ring, promises a fortune to be made.
explanation.walkthrough: Fortune looks like money to be earned; it is fortune as in fortune-telling.
explanation.definitionFit: A horoscope is an astrological forecast, the source of a reading of one's fortune or destiny.

clue.text: Heavy metal bar?

parts.note: surface reading: a pub where rock fans drink
setter's reading: a cast block of a dense metal such as gold or lead

explanation.walkthrough: Heavy metal suggests loud rock music, and bar a pub; read literally it is a bar of weighty metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingots are cast blocks of metal, typically gold, which is notably dense and heavy.
